technical_and_design_decisions: Use Spring Boot's @SpringBootTest and JUnit 5 for acceptance tests, leveraging existing Spring test infrastructure.
For modules requiring external services (e.g., Splunk), use Testcontainers to provide lightweight, disposable instances.
For the spark-app batch job, use Spark local mode to run acceptance tests without a full cluster.
For the timestampfile batch job, leverage Spring Batch's test utilities and temporary file systems.
Integrate all acceptance tests into the existing CI pipeline (e.g., GitHub Actions) as a separate test stage.
Use Maven or Gradle build profiles to conditionally run acceptance tests only when changes affect the relevant modules.
assumptions: The source code for all modules (null sink, rich_gauge sink, router sink, shell sink, splunk sink, throughput-sampler sink, spark-app batch, timestampfile batch) already exists and is part of the same Spring project.
The project uses a standard build system (Maven or Gradle) and has an existing CI pipeline that can be extended.
Acceptance tests are defined as integration-level tests that verify end-to-end behavior (e.g., input -> module -> output).
Each module is well-documented or the developer has sufficient understanding of its functionality from prior work or code inspection.
The necessary test dependencies (Testcontainers, Spark test libraries, etc.) are already available or can be added without significant overhead.
No external infrastructure changes (e.g., new CI servers) are required beyond adding new test steps.
